title: Mulch and enrich the soil of established landscaped areas

lessons.title: Feeding the soil with compost and manure
lessons.html:
Feeding the soil with compost and manure

Good soil makes healthy plants. Soil is not just dirt. It is full of small living things, like earthworms, that help plants grow. Over time, soil in a garden becomes poor and hard. We make it rich again by adding organic matter, such as compost and old manure.

What organic matter does

  • It feeds the plants slowly.
  • It helps sandy soil hold water.
  • It makes clay soil softer, so roots and water can go in.
  • It feeds earthworms and other soil life.

Types of organic matter

MaterialNotes
CompostMade from rotted leaves, grass clippings and plant waste. Dark and crumbly.
Kraal manureFrom cattle. Use it old and well-rotted, not fresh.
Chicken manureVery strong. Use only a little, as your team leader says.
Leaf mouldRotted leaves; good for shade beds.

Fresh manure can burn plants and may carry weed seeds. Always use old, rotted manure.

How to enrich an established bed

  1. Pull out weeds first.
  2. Water the bed if it is very dry.
  3. Spread a layer of compost on top of the soil, around the plants, as thick as your team leader says.
  4. Keep compost away from the stems of plants.
  5. Gently fork it into the top of the soil. Do not dig deep near plants. You will cut their roots.
  6. Water well.

Wear gloves when you work with manure and compost. Wash your hands well afterwards, and cover any cuts on your skin.

lessons.title: Mulching beds
lessons.html:
Mulching beds

Mulch is a layer of material put on top of the soil. It covers the soil like a blanket.

Why we mulch

  • It keeps water in the soil, so we water less.
  • It keeps the soil cool in summer and warm in winter.
  • It stops many weeds from growing.
  • It stops rain from washing the soil away.
  • Organic mulch slowly rots and feeds the soil.
  • It makes the bed look neat.

Types of mulch

  • Organic mulch: bark chips, wood chips, pine needles, straw, dry grass clippings, compost.
  • Inorganic mulch: gravel, small stones, pebbles. Good for succulent and waterwise gardens.

How to mulch

  1. Weed the bed well. Mulch on top of weeds does not work.
  2. Water the soil first, so it is damp under the mulch.
  3. Spread the mulch evenly over the bed, to the thickness your team leader tells you.
  4. Leave a small gap around the stems of plants and trunks of trees. Mulch against stems makes them rot.
  5. Keep mulch off paths and lawns. Rake the edges neat.
  6. Top up the mulch when it gets thin, usually once or twice a year.

Do not

  • Do not use thick fresh grass clippings. They go slimy and smelly. Dry them first.
  • Do not use plant material with weed seeds or diseases.
  • Do not pile mulch high against walls of houses.

Safety

Bags of bark and compost are heavy. Bend your knees and keep your back straight. Use a wheelbarrow. Wear gloves; bark chips can give splinters.

Key points

  • Compost and old manure make soil richer and better at holding water.
  • Never use fresh manure; it burns plants.
  • Mulch keeps water in, stops weeds and protects soil.
  • Weed and water before mulching.
  • Keep mulch and compost away from stems and trunks.
